title: What does student safety mean in a more hostile world?
summary: When a far-right march was planned near her flat, her university said nothing. Cynthia Keza Birikundavyi argues that setting a threshold for communication is an administrative adjustment, not a political act
full_text:
On Saturday 18 April 2026, I got to brunch 30 minutes late.

My preparation was derailed by a text from a friend warning me that a far-right march expecting over a thousand people was going to start by my flat. It was the second one in two months.

Emptiness, frustration, non-surprise, and a small sting of self-reproach for having let my guard down rushed through me. I let it settle for a second, before having to neatly repack all I was feeling.

An hour later, over eggs and French toast, I shared the reasons for my delay, with animated revolt and sarcastic laughter, the way you do when you are trying not to show yet another scar that has been reopened before it had a chance to heal.

The first time I was told Britain First planned a gathering a few hundred metres from my door, I did what others would do – I looked online. The information was sparse, fragmented across local news and social media.

So I waited for my university to say something. When nothing came, I went to my students’ union, before seeking information from academic staff. The response I received framed the event as outside the university’s purview because it was off-campus.

So I ended up moving through that Saturday without guidance, relying on educated guesswork to decide how to safely find my way around my own city.

Right to safety

After the weekend had passed, deciding that the careful, considered version of my frustration deserved the most senior audience I could find, I wrote to the head of security and the vice president with clear questions on how the university determines the thresholds for what warrants communication to keep its students safe.

The response was swift and thoughtful. Senior leadership acknowledged that the gap between institutional process and lived student experience was real. They recognised that while public events in Manchester city centre do not automatically fall within the university’s operational remit, the impact on students whose experience extends well beyond the physical boundaries of the campus does.

They expressed willingness to review how the university assesses foreseeable student impact. The machinery of institutional reflection, it seemed, had been set in motion.

Less than two months later came a bigger march, a larger police presence, and the same silence. This time, I did not know until the morning of.

People organising in large numbers because they do not want you here is a very particular kind of violence. It is something that, unfortunately, some of us have had to get used to. But the specific, corporeal knowing that hundreds of people have invested time, money, and something far more venomous to protest your presence is an eerie feeling, hard to describe, and harder to live with.

Over the twelve years since I was last a student in the UK, the relationship between the state and the migrant student has hardened. To come back, I have satisfied every condition this system has placed on my presence. I have my Right to Rent. I have my Right to Study. On these two occasions, I could not find my Right to Safety.

I am not asking universities to resolve the structural conditions that make racist mobilisations possible, and I understand that institutions cannot neutralise the environments they operate in. What they can do, however, is know enough about those environments, and the people moving through them, to build the conditions that mean no one has to face it alone.

That is not politics. That is duty of care.

The yes, but reflex

I cannot know what internal conversations took place between February and April, but I have sat in enough institutional meetings to recognise the shape of what happens between private acknowledgment and public silence. It is a phenomenon I have come to think of as the “Yes, But” reflex.

Yes, we care about student safety. But this event is not on university property. Yes, we understand the impact on marginalised students, but if we communicate about this march, do we have to communicate about every protest? Where do we draw the line? Yes, we want to be ahead of the issue, but what if our communication is interpreted as endorsing a counter-protest? What if we expose ourselves to legal risk?

Each “Yes, But” is a small, reasonable-sounding step away from action, and each one is defensible in isolation. Cumulatively, they form a wall of institutional caution that treats the university as a legal entity first and a community of care second, and it can make the management of liability feel more visible than the fulfilment of duty.

A red herring

The fear of setting a precedent is a red herring, because thresholds can be defined based on proximity, scale, and impact on the student population. This is not a conceptual leap so much as an administrative adjustment.

What happened outside my flat in February and April was not an aberration, and any institution treating it as one is planning for a world that has already gone. HOPE not hate counted 251 anti-migrant events across 77 locations in the second half of 2025 alone, and what started as a local flashpoint in Epping has hardened into a repertoire – hotel pickets, flag campaigns, vigilante patrols – that can be assembled in almost any town in the country within days.

The universities that handle this year well will be the ones deciding now, in September, what their threshold for communication is and who owns the decision, rather than the ones drafting a statement on the morning of a march while the phones are already ringing.

That preparation also means being clear on what communication does, and does not, amount to. And I should be clear here: telling students that a protest may affect their safety or wellbeing, and giving them practical information to navigate it does not make the university a participant in the politics of that protest. A lawful demonstration in a city centre is lawful, and nothing I have described asks a university to prevent one, to police what is said at it, or to take a position on whether it should happen at all.

The problem comes when caution around freedom of speech becomes caution around communication itself. Collapsing the two is how institutions talk themselves into believing that saying nothing is the neutral option. It is not neutral. Silence is an institutional choice and its consequences on the student community are not borne equally.

Given that in England, the regulator is consulting on free speech guidance as I write, it would be a poor outcome if the effect were to make providers more nervous about giving students the information they need to move safely through the places they live and study.

Already waiting in her inbox

Institutional silence has a cost. It costs peace, it costs focus, and it costs the hours spent writing this instead of the research I came here to do. And it costs something harder to recover than time – the confidence that my university stands behind its own words.

Nevertheless, without proactive action we will manage, out of necessity, to handle these situations alone. When the next protest comes, we will adjust our routes and keep our heads down, relying once again on the informal networks that remind us through their care that our full membership in this community is not a burden.

In the meantime? Well, I am speaking up again. In the hope that the next time a student like me wakes up to a text message warning of a march against her existence, a university email is already waiting in her inbox, reminding her that her institution has her back.

title: WEEKEND READING: Part One: Experience of loneliness of incoming students
summary:

The post WEEKEND READING: Part One: Experience of loneliness of incoming students appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Dr Michelle Morgan, Dean of Students, University of East London and Dr David Gilani, Head of Access and Participation, Middlesex University

We know from numerous reports, including the UK Covid-19 Inquiry, Research on the measurement of loneliness and Cognitive testing of loneliness by the Office for National Statistics, that loneliness is prevalent in the UK. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) research showed that 33% of Britons aged 16 to 29 reported feeling lonely “often, always or some of the time”.

What is the prevalence of loneliness for new undergraduate and postgraduate taught (includes PG Certs/Diplomas, Masters and other PGT ) entrants starting university, and what can we do about it?

This is one of the many areas explored in the Pre-arrival Academic Questionnaire Pilot in England, funded by the Office for Students and led by Advance HE, Jisc and the University of East London. Phase one of the two-year project undertaken across fifteen institutions comprised of 5,548 undergraduate and 2,285 postgraduate taught completions.

Four questions were included. The first three questions were from the UCLA three-item loneliness scale, which is currently used in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing , and the last is a direct question about how often the respondent feels lonely, currently used in the Community Life Survey. The questions were:

How often do you feel that you lack companionship?

How often do you feel left out?

How often do you feel isolated from others?

How often do you feel lonely?

And the response categories: Hardly ever or never / Some of the time / Often

The four questions have been analysed by key student characteristics across undergraduate and postgraduate taught levels of study. It is important to recognise and understand how our students feel so we can support them effectively within their university life.

What did the pilot find?

Domiciled status

When examined by domicile status and level of study, Non-UK undergraduate (UG) and postgraduate taught (PGT) students selected ‘some of the time’ more frequently for all four questions compared to UK UG and PGT (see Table 1). Lacked companionship was the loneliness marker that was most frequently selected by all groups.

When looking at the questions respondents selected ‘Often’ for, UK UG and PGT reported higher levels of loneliness than Non-UK UG and PGT, citing Felt lonely most frequently.

Table 1 Domiciled status by level of study ‘Some of the time’ and ‘Often’ responses

Sex

When sex is examined by the ‘Some of the time’ response, Lacked companionship was cited the most by both UG and PGT Females and Males (see Table 2). For ‘Often’ responses, Felt lonely was cited the most by both Females and Male undergraduates. However, at the postgraduate taught level, Felt isolated was cited most by Females, while for Males it was Felt lonely.

Table 2 Sex by level of study ‘Some of the time’ and ‘Often’ responses

COVID-19 study experience

The experience of the COVID-19 pandemic is still being felt by incoming undergraduate students, as the Pre-arrival questionnaire (PAQ) national pilot wave 1 initial results highlight. Responses for ‘Some of the time’ and ‘Often’ were higher for those in study during the pandemic than those who were not (see Table 3). Again Lacked companionship was most cited for the ‘Some of the time’ response and for ‘Often’ it was Felt lonely.

Table 3 Undergraduate and study status during the COVID-19 pandemic and ‘Some of the time’ and ‘Often’ responses

Undergraduate attendance in previous study

When prior study attendance of incoming undergraduates was examined, the frequence that ‘Often’ was cited across the four questions increased as attendance decreased (see Figure 1). As numbers from the Department of Education highlight, Pupil absence in schools in England continues to rise, with 150,000 children classed as severely absent, so this behavioural experience and impact on loneliness will continue.

Estranged and care experience

When the responses of those who are estranged from their family or who have care experience are examined, loneliness levels amongst those who have care experience are higher across all four questions than for those that do not (See Tables 3 and 4). Again, across both groups, Lacked companionship is the highest for ‘Some of the time’ and for ‘Often’ the most frequent response is Felt lonely.

These findings reflect those found in the Unite Foundation report Unseen and under pressure: the academic experience of estranged and care-experienced students (a report that took a deep dive into the HEPI and Advance HE Student Academic Experience Survey 2025).

Table 3 Estranged status and loneliness

Table 4 Care experienced and loneliness

Age

For both undergraduate and postgraduate taught responses, levels of loneliness across all questions are higher amongst 18 to 24 year olds than other age groups. This reflects the research of Professor Andrea Wigfield, Director of the Centre for Loneliness Studies at Sheffield Hallam University, which shows loneliness is higher amongst adults between 18 and 24.

However, when we looking specifically at the loneliness levels of postgraduate taught students, ‘Often’ Feeling lonely was higher across the age groups up to 25 and 36-40 year olds (see Figure 3).

Ethnicity

When Ethnicity responses are examined, there were no notable differences amongst PGT respondents, but there were at UG level. Mixed and White Ethnic groups reported the highest levels of feeling loneliness ‘Often’. Within each group, Felt lonely was the highest across four of the groups.

Table 5 Type of Ethnicity ‘Often’ Loneliness by undergraduate level

Disability

When examined by disability across health, mental and physical disabilities, it will not be a surprise to see that levels of feeling lonely ‘Often’ are higher for those with disabilities than for those who do not have one. Again, this reflects the findings found in the Office for National Statistics Disability, well-being and loneliness, UK – Office for National Statistics and the UK Government Disability, loneliness and relationships reports.

When different disabilities were explored, there were notable differences by both type of disability and level of study (see Table 6).

Undergraduate loneliness responses were higher than postgraduate taught across all questions but one, with physical disability having the highest ‘Often’ responses. For PGT, Lack of companionship was the highest amongst those with a mental disability, Felt left out and Felt lonely was highest amongst those with a health disability, and for Felt isolated it was those with physical disabilities who reported this most frequently.

Table 6 Type of disability ‘Often’ Loneliness’ by level of study

Summary

This blog highlights the complexity of ‘loneliness’ across a range of student characteristics. As Dr Gareth Hughes, Clinical Lead for Student Space, says when talking about overcoming loneliness at university:

loneliness is a normal human response to the absence of something we need. It’s like feeling hungry as a response to needing food. Loneliness is simply a warning sign that we need to act to improve our social connections.

Part two, will look at the assumptions about loneliness and belonging that the sector is at risk of making, and will suggest practical steps institutions can take to mitigate these risks to help navigate the ‘loneliness’ journey at university by improving social connections throughout the study journey.

title: European education powerhouses rocked by falling scores in global study
summary:
France and Germany among countries with low Pisa scores, which show how well 15-year-olds use school learning in life

France’s were its worst ever. Germany’s, too. In the Netherlands, results also tumbled to all-time lows. Even in Finland, Europe’s much-vaunted schools champion and a global leader for decades, scores plummeted.

The 2025 Pisa scores, which assess how effectively 15-year-olds apply school-learned knowledge and skills in reading, mathematics and science to real-life situations, have rocked some of western Europe’s education powerhouses.

Continue reading...
full_text:
France’s were its worst ever. Germany’s, too. In the Netherlands, results also tumbled to all-time lows. Even in Finland, Europe’s much-vaunted schools champion and a global leader for decades, scores plummeted.

The 2025 Pisa scores, which assess how effectively 15-year-olds apply school-learned knowledge and skills in reading, mathematics and science to real-life situations, have rocked some of western Europe’s education powerhouses.

While the UK bucked the trend, results on the continent continued a slide that began in 2018. In France, Germany, the Netherlands and Finland, the proportion of 15-year-olds lacking basic functional literacy and maths skills rose to nearly one in three.

Pandemic learning losses accelerated the drop, but education experts say the roots of the problem run much deeper: chronic teacher shortages, repeated curriculum reforms that have neglected basic skills and widening inequalities within increasingly segregated systems.

Compounding it all, incessant smartphone use has dramatically reduced attention spans, replacing “deep reading” with scrolling, and pupil motivation has collapsed.

Pupils in Germany got their worst-ever Pisa report card, reviving a decades-old debate about the country’s weaknesses in schools, integration and closing the wealth gap. Samuel Greiff, the German Pisa study coordinator, noted an alarming rise in youngsters who lack basic skills for citizenship and employment, including the ability to understand a written text and do rudimentary consumer maths.

The study found that in Europe’s top economy the link between academic performance and socioeconomic status was particularly strong: only 2% of pupils from low-income families achieve high levels of competence, against 25% from higher-income families – a correlation twice as strong as in Denmark or Norway.

“Other countries are far more successful in decoupling educational success from family background,” Greiff told local media, noting that class had a far greater influence on teens’ academic success than whether their family had immigrated.

Germany endured a first “Pisa-Schock” in 2000, when the report’s dismal ratings triggered a nationwide effort to raise performance. The 2012 report identified significant improvement, putting the country above the OECD average.

But the 2025 edition showed Germany slipping back to average, with about one in four pupils lacking competency in natural sciences and one in three in reading and maths. About one in five demonstrated insufficient capabilities in all three areas.

The number of teens deemed “at risk” because they lacked the reading and maths skills for further education has doubled over the last decade, and reading for pleasure has declined at a faster rate in Germany than in other industrialised countries: one in two 15-year-olds said they only read when it was required.

Strikingly, pupils from the most socioeconomically privileged neighbourhoods recorded the sharpest decline in reading comprehension. Education minister Karin Prien said the report required an urgent response, highlighting the negative influence of excessive social media use and pledging to present new measures to protect younger children by the end of the year.

In the Netherlands, the scores marked a historic low point, setting troubling new records in reading literacy, where a record 39% of 15-year-olds now lack the basic skills required to navigate modern society, evaluate the credibility of sources or process multi-page texts, up from 33% in the previous 2022 edition.

Researchers noted that the Dutch reading score has plunged by more than 60 points over the last decade, meaning today’s 15-year-olds are effectively reading at the level that 12-year-olds achieved 10 years ago.

The decline was less marked in maths, where Dutch pupils once dominated the European rankings, but still represented a record low only marginally higher than the OECD average, while the science score was also below its previous level.

The Dutch education ministry promised urgent action, acknowledging that the assessment “confirms our decline was not a temporary post-pandemic dip, but a structural issue. We can’t accept a society where a third of our youth leave school unprepared for basic reading in daily life.”

However, teachers’ unions and literacy advocates reacted with frustration. The AOb teachers’ union argued reading levels would never improve as long as “classes are routinely cancelled, non-qualified staff are filling gaps, and the workload is driving experienced educators out of the profession.”

The reading advocacy group Stichting Lezen added that the failure lay “not with pupils, but with an approach that has turned reading into a set of mechanical comprehension tricks rather than fostering deep reading habits”.

In France, the scores were similarly grim. “It’s worrying, but it’s unfortunately not a surprise,” said Édouard Geffray, the education minister. Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate, called the outcome a “catastrophe” and a reflection of the nation’s decline.

French education analysts have long warned of a lack of state investment, particularly in primary schools, as well as a highly unequal system where socioeconomic status dictates results, while governments have tended to approach education failings by debating timetabling and how many hours children sit at their desks.

Over the past decade, a succession of eight different education ministers has resulted in constant policy changes and reversals, leaving teachers feeling more stressed by the avalanche of directives than by teaching in class. Mid-career salaries, meanwhile, remain below the OECD average and another recent report found just 4% of French teachers felt valued.

Éric Charbonnier, an OECD education analyst, argued that the focus should shift away from debates over desk hours toward greater autonomy to explore teaching methods, and more method-focused training.

In Finland, average results were lower than in 2022 in maths and reading, and stable in science. Dr Arto K Ahonen, Pisa national project manager at the Finnish Institute for Educational Research, said the results had prompted serious discussion over pupils’ perseverance and effort.

“The goal remains to reverse the decline and return to a rising trend,” Ahonen said. “Meanwhile, we recognise the universal decline we are part of.”

Ahonen noted that the Finnish system had seen “no major change in our education system in 50 years,” warning that “curricula must be renewed as times and society change. It’s unlikely that any school system could operate with the same curricula for decades, even a successful one.”

In neighbouring Sweden, record-low results spurred heated political debate ahead of recent elections, with party leaders blaming everything from screens to immigration and insufficient teaching staff. But experts say there is no single explanation.

In its report on the latest scores, Skolverket, the national education agency, said several changes were already under way aimed at reinforcing pupils’ knowledge and the classroom role of teachers in creating a “safer and more equal environment”.

title: Report: Student Protections Haven’t Kept Up With Higher Ed’s Adoption of AI
summary:
Report: Student Protections Haven’t Kept Up With Higher Ed’s Adoption of AI
Olivia.sanchez Fri, 09/18/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
Artificial intelligence has wormed its way into almost every aspect of college operations, from admissions and hiring to teaching and learning. The technology may have the power to revolutionize higher education, but protections for students haven’t kept pace with innovation, according to a new report from Student Defense’s SHAPE—Safeguarding Higher-Ed Through AI Practices & Ethics—AI initiative.

In the report, Students at Stake: Risks of AI Deployment in Higher Education, higher education leaders and researchers say they are concerned about how AI is used, specifically in admissions, student services and education delivery. They identify risks related to bias; data privacy; the loss of learning communities; and disclosure, transparency and credibility.

Dan Zibel, co-founder and chief counsel of Student Defense, said in a statement that leaders “cannot afford to adopt AI first and ask questions later.”

“The pursuit of higher education involves some of the most consequential decisions a student can make. Although certain uses of AI have tremendous potential, colleges and universities must understand the risks, establish clear guardrails, and ensure strong student protections keep pace with the technology,” Zibel said. “At a time when many Americans are questioning the value of a college degree, strong institutional governance is necessary to ensure that colleges are using AI only to add value, rather than cheapening the educational experience.”

Using AI in admissions, recruitment and financial aid raises concerns about which students are contacted by colleges, what messages they’re receiving, how aid is distributed and whether students understand the true cost of college, the authors write. Unchecked use could lead to misleading representations, discriminatory targeting or manipulation of student choice.

The use of AI in advising, counseling and student services is especially risky, they note; it could encourage students to be particularly vulnerable and potentially expose them to incorrect guidance or result in other academic or financial consequences.

AI could also negatively impact the delivery of education, including the quality of teaching, academic freedom and student privacy, according to the report.

The report advises college leaders to ask themselves specific questions before implementing AI products: What problem are we trying to solve? Do we have adequate policies and governance structures in place to ensure functionality, guarantee accountability and manage risks? Are we being transparent? Is this creating value for students?

“Human judgment and behavior are also imperfect. But the speed, power, and probabilistic nature of AI can amplify risks in ways that are difficult to understand,” the report says. “These risks persist even when the technology appears to function flawlessly yet contains errors—such as hallucinations—that produce mistakes a human substitute would be unlikely to make.”

In response to the report, U.S. Congresswoman Suzanne Bonamici, an Oregon Democrat, said in a statement that AI in higher education shouldn’t be a substitute for critical thinking and implementation of the technology should be grounded in ethics, transparency and fairness.

“As colleges and universities expand their use of AI, students and educators need clear guardrails and resources so this technology can expand opportunities, not widen gaps,” Bonamici said.

title: Private Minn. University to Receive $82M for Low-Income, First-Gen Programs
summary:
Private Minn. University to Receive $82M for Low-Income, First-Gen Programs
Olivia.sanchez Fri, 09/18/2026 - 03:00 AM

The gift will boost student scholarships and fund centers for first-generation students and leadership.

Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
The University of St. Thomas in Minnesota on Thursday announced an $82 million gift to support low-income and first-generation students. The donation, from the Ciresi Walburn Foundation and the Michael V. and Ann C. Ciresi Foundation, is the largest in the private Catholic university’s 141-year history, and is part of a $1 billion fundraising campaign.

The gift will establish a Center for First-Generation Students and a Center for Leadership and will fund the existing Ciresi Walburn Leadership Fellows Program for low-income students in perpetuity, according to the foundation.

The fellowship program was created in 2022 for Black male students, who make up less than 9 percent of St. Thomas’s student body. But like many institutional programs once designed for a particular demographic group, it now accepts students of any race and gender—a change many colleges and universities have implemented under pressure from anti-DEI state and federal lawmakers, who argue that the Supreme Court’s ban on the consideration of race in admissions should extend to scholarship and grant programs.

Now, the main criterion for Ciresi fellows is demonstrated financial need and a commitment to service and social justice, according to a statement from the university. Candidates don’t have to have a certain grade point average or be enrolled in a particular field of study, but they do have to agree to meet regularly and attend professional development activities and employer site visits throughout the year. In return, they can receive up to $17,500 in scholarship money per year, or $70,000 over four years. The scholarship doesn’t cover everything; the university estimates the total cost of attendance is nearly $78,000, including tuition, fees, housing, food and other expenses.

Although the program is relatively new, leaders say they’ve seen promising results so far. Of the 10 students in the first fellowship cohort, nine graduated within four years and one is on track to graduate in five years, according to Daniel Sellers, executive director of the Ciresi Walburn Foundation.

Sellers said the program began when university leaders and the foundation realized that low-income students left the university in their first two years at higher rates than their peers.

“Finances alone were not the cause of them deciding not to continue at St. Thomas. That, of course, was part of it. But there’s so much more,” Sellers said. “There’s a desire for a sense of belonging, a desire to find affinity with others on campus and support when, invariably, challenges appear.”

Roberta Walburn, trustee of the Ciresi Walburn Foundation, said in a statement that the donation and the future centers for leadership and first-generation students will give students and community members the chance “to learn from one another and lead meaningful change.”

“The fellows have shown us what is possible when talented young people receive not only financial support, but also the networks, experiences and opportunities they need to become confident and effective leaders,” Walburn said.

Lily Asrat, director of the fellows program, said that when students are relieved of financial stress, it allows them to focus on academics, get involved on campus and pursue internships. The scholarship money, paired with mentorship and peer support, “is really there to make sure they thrive,” she said.

“So many issues around retention with first-gen students and students of high financial need [are because] they don’t have all the safety nets and social supports that many other students have,” Asrat said. The fellowship program gives the students “people and support that will catch them when they fall.”

Junior marketing major Terrell J. Cummings joined the program halfway through his freshman year, at which point he said, “I was a C-plus student first semester, and a little knucklehead.”

Once Cummings started spending time around people who believed in him, his mindset shifted. He said he started getting better grades and is now the student vice president for the program.

The program’s leaders and his peers are “pushing me to be the man I’m becoming now,” he said. He expects to graduate in 2028.

The community he’s found, paired with the professional development opportunities and scholarship, “is honestly just the catalyst of what Black excellence looks like.”

title: UT Austin Axes Several Ethnic, Gender Studies Majors
summary:
UT Austin Axes Several Ethnic, Gender Studies Majors
Emma Whitford Fri, 09/18/2026 - 03:00 AM

Some faculty members consider the decision the next step in a broader effort to gut what remains of ethnic and gender studies at the university.

Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
full_text:
The University of Texas at Austin will eliminate four majors—African and African diaspora studies; Mexican American and Latina/o studies; women’s and gender studies; and race, indigeneity and migration—as the university continues to overhaul its undergraduate curriculum and whittle down its ethnic and gender studies programs. Faculty members in the newly consolidated Social and Culture Analysis Department, which housed those majors, say they received no explanation as to why they are being cut, but some consider the move part of an ongoing effort to gradually gut the department and censor students’ learning.

Danielle Clealand, interim chair of the SCA department, told faculty members on Tuesday that the provost’s office “rejected our proposal to keep our majors,” according to an email shared with Inside Higher Ed. Interim Dean of the College of Liberal Arts Dan Brinks suggested the department instead create an “ethnic studies major with tracks or a SCA major with tracks,” Clealand wrote.

The urban studies and American studies majors, which also fall under the SCA umbrella, will remain, though faculty are confused as to whether American studies is accepting new students at this time. UT Austin students apply to a specific major at the university, and The Austin-American Statesman reported Thursday that students currently applying to UT for next fall do not see an option to add ethnic studies or gender studies as a primary or secondary major. American studies is also missing, the Statesman reported. In an emailed statement to Inside Higher Ed on Thursday, university spokesperson Mike Rosen said that the American studies and urban studies majors remain intact.

“In recognition of the changing degree offerings in the Department of Social and Cultural Analysis, the University is no longer enrolling new students in three majors: Mexican American and Latina/o Studies, African and African Diaspora Studies, and Women’s & Gender Studies. So, as you might expect, those majors have been removed from the University’s admissions applications to avoid new students enrolling in majors that are changing,” Rosen wrote. “Students currently enrolled in those majors will be able to complete their degree. The Department is encouraged to develop a new degree proposal that represents its combined academic interests. American Studies and Urban Studies majors remain.”

Faculty members in the SCA department came up with a new major over the summer that would replace the race, indigeneity and migration major, but they are currently re-evaluating it in light of the recent eliminations.

Julie Minich, who teaches literature and Mexican American and Latina/o studies, said she was not surprised the majors were rejected but “was still shocked.”

“We had all been fearing it, but it just seemed so beyond the pale,” Minich said. “To me, it’s just such blatant censorship, such blatant viewpoint discrimination.”

For American studies professor Lauren Gutterman, the decision to ax the legacy majors represents the next step in the university administration’s slow march to close ethnic and gender studies programs. When she and her colleagues learned in February that their various departments were being folded into one, they were told “that consolidation would be a way for us to continue doing the teaching and research we’ve always done,” Gutterman said.

But since then, the university has taken several more steps to minimize the programs and to make it easier to shutter them entirely. In May, the University of Texas system established that presidents could bypass typical review procedures and close academic programs in “extraordinary circumstances” that necessitate “accelerated program closure due to regulatory requirements.” The new rules also allow a president to eliminate faculty positions for “bona fide academic reasons,” which include “poor program quality or effectiveness, misalignment with the institution’s mission, failure to meet student or societal needs, low enrollment and demand, and redundancy with other existing more effective programs.”

At the time, faculty feared the policy changes would allow universities to shutter departments for political reasons.

Three months later, UT Austin unveiled its new core curriculum, which booted several SCA classes from the core, Gutterman said. Then, earlier this month, the provost’s office announced that core courses in newly consolidated departments—SCA and the new Department of European and Eurasian Studies—would “no longer automatically” retain their spot in the core curriculum starting this spring, according to an email shared with Inside Higher Ed.

“Only the two new consolidated departments were given this special treatment, and all of our courses were automatically removed from the core starting in the spring,” Gutterman said.

Now, the SCA department is left with few existing majors and no current core courses.

“I think that what this is setting us up for is a mass firing of faculty, because already the UT Board of Regents passed the policy making it much easier to fire faculty regardless of tenure status if they shut down the program or department that you’re in, and then if we go from having multiple degree programs to having one or two, the university leaders could easily say, ‘We don’t need all these faculty to staff this one degree program,’” Gutterman said.

Minich agreed.

“It really feels like we are being sabotaged,” she said. “We’re a new department, and we are being set up to fail.”

Both Minich and Gutterman said the decisions amounted to censorship of students, who often seek out SCA disciplines as secondary majors that will aid them in working with and serving a diverse Texas population when they enter the workforce.

“The censorship that’s happening at Texas A&M and Texas Tech has been much more explicit and direct, saying, ‘You can’t teach courses about race, gender, sexuality.’ Here, what we’re experiencing is an attack on our courses through administrative means,” Gutterman said. “So it might seem less motivated by politics, but the motivations are exactly the same. The mechanism is different, and it is still censorship.”

title: U of Austin Won’t Seek ABA Accreditation for Legal Program
summary:
U of Austin Won’t Seek ABA Accreditation for Legal Program
Ryan Quinn Fri, 09/18/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Ryan Quinn
full_text:
The University of Austin, a five-year-old institution founded by CBS News Editor in Chief Bari Weiss and others, says it won’t seek the American Bar Association Accreditation Council’s recognition for its legal program.

UATX, which first accepted students in fall 2024, doesn’t yet have institutional accreditation, though it’s seeking it.

The institution’s announcement comes after the Education Department recommended last month that the ABA Council lose federal recognition to accredit law schools, meaning its accreditation wouldn't unlock federal student aid for those schools. Some Republican-controlled states have also targeted the ABA Council, which has received criticism for its past support of diversity, equity and inclusion. Earlier this year, the Texas Supreme Court allowed lawyers who haven’t graduated from ABA Council–accredited schools to practice in the state.

In a lengthy Substack post Thursday, UATX General Counsel Adam Biggs condemned the ABA.

“The ABA is a private trade association that has spent seventy years making sure no one builds a law school that doesn’t conform to its exact vision for legal education,” Biggs wrote, adding that the “model it enforces is expensive and outdated, and it stifles anyone who tries to build something different.”

He said UATX will partner with the conservative Federalist Society in its undergraduate legal education, supporting courses “that go further into the Constitution’s text, history, and tradition, taught by judges, practicing lawyers, and scholars.”

He criticized ABA standards in detail, including requirements for tenured positions. He said the standards also “make creating [legal] clinics largely unavoidable.”

“Students working real cases sounds good, in the abstract,” Biggs wrote. “Yet it is the most expensive way to teach anything. A professor teaching Property reaches hundreds of students. A clinical professor works with about eight.”

He further blamed the “ABA-enforced pipeline” for left-leaning faculty and student bodies at law schools and said the legal clinics themselves overwhelmingly support left-leaning causes. He denounced a “grievance-based study of the law [that] undermines the pursuit of truth and instills the belief that the Constitution and our republic are obstacles to be torn down.”

Attacking the cost of legal education, he also said, “Someone called to serve ordinary Americans and work in public-interest law shouldn’t have to abandon that calling because only a large-firm salary can service the loans.”

In an emailed statement, Melissa Hart, chair of the ABA Council, said it accredits law schools “with a wide range of missions and perspectives” that “innovate in all aspects of their program, setting minimum standards that lead to strong outcomes.”

“States also recognize other law schools that—for a variety of reasons—do not choose to pursue Council accreditation. That system of combining national accreditation, which ensures degree portability, with parallel pathways to practice has worked well for many years, and it will continue to as the University of Austin builds its program,” she said.

title: A Kinda, Sorta Requirement
summary:
A Kinda, Sorta Requirement
Sara Brady Fri, 09/18/2026 - 03:00 AM

Students don’t do optional—but sometimes they also don’t do required.

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
We had a conversation in the deans’ weekly meeting that got me wondering how other colleges have solved (or not solved) a dilemma.

The topic was developmental English. Right now, if students place into it (which most don’t), it’s a corequisite for the first composition course. The idea is to use it to offer extra support to students who need it to raise their game in composition. Rather than teaching skills in the abstract and in isolation, they can be geared toward the assignments in the credit-bearing class. It’s a model that gets students on the degree path right away, and that has shown better success than a stand-alone course. So far, so good.

But students don’t always behave in the ways we expect them to.

Requiring the course for the students who place into it ensures that it’s eligible for financial aid. It also greatly increases the chances that students will attend faithfully. As Kay McClenney noted years ago, students don’t do optional.

So, what should we do when students who were required to take the support class fail the support class but pass the college-level class?

It’s a conflict between the letter of the law and the spirit of the law. But when financial aid hangs in the balance, we have to be particularly careful. That’s especially true in a political climate in which certain actors are looking for excuses to attack.

Philosophically, it seems clear that a student who felt misplaced, didn’t bother showing up for the developmental class and then passed the credit-bearing class proved their point. We thought they needed the extra help, but they proved otherwise. The educator in me wants to say more power to ’em.

By the letter of the policy, though, failing the developmental class means losing eligibility for the corequisite course. (That’s literally what “corequisite” means.) If the student isn’t eligible for the second class, then they’re disqualified, even if their performance indicates passing work.

I’d prefer to make the developmental class recommended, as opposed to required, but “students don’t do optional” suggests that rendering it optional will mean that many students who could have used the help would skip it. The tutoring center provides a sort of confirmation. Far fewer students go for tutoring—which is free—than would likely benefit from it. We let students know about tutoring, it’s easy to find on campus and the spot is pleasant and welcoming, but uptake remains stubbornly low relative to apparent need.

Financial aid adds another wrinkle. Optional courses aren’t eligible for financial aid coverage. Even if we convinced the right students that the class would be beneficial, it wouldn’t count toward their financial aid. Selling them on a class they couldn’t afford wouldn’t do anyone any good.

Of course, if community college were free, we could easily allow students waivers for the coreq if they passed the higher-level class without worrying about financial aid. But in this world, that’s not an option.

All that said, there’s no way that we’re the only college facing this dilemma.

title: ‘Direct Repression’ of Academics on the Rise, Report Finds
summary:
‘Direct Repression’ of Academics on the Rise, Report Finds
Susan H. Greenberg Fri, 09/18/2026 - 03:00 AM

Universities must promote “broad public understanding” that university autonomy is essential, Scholars at Risk’s annual report says.

Byline(s)
Georgia Luckhurst for Times Higher Education
full_text:
Universities in democracies such as Georgia, India and the United States have seen their autonomy “violated” by government interference in the past year, according to the latest annual update from the international academic rights organization Scholars at Risk.

Free to Think 2026 documents 382 attacks on scholars, students and institutions in 59 countries and territories between July 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026.

The figure is marginally down from last year’s tally of 395 such attacks, despite an increase in the number of countries and territories evaluated, from 49 last year to 59 this year. But the differences are not merely numerical.

Last year’s report noted attacks by police forces on protesting students in Bangladesh, which led to thousands of injuries and the deaths of up to 1,400 people. It also flagged cuts to international aid and collaboration, such as the U.S. government’s cuts to research funding, which affected research projects and educational opportunities abroad, in countries from Afghanistan and Malawi to Australia and Portugal.

This year’s findings point to the “direct repression and overt violence” seen in the form of wrongful imprisonment of academics in China and Russia, and even the “targeted assassinations” of university leaders in Guatemala and Pakistan.

But even countries better associated with academic freedom have undergone legislative and administrative shifts “to restrict higher education systems,” the report reads.

In the U.S., for instance, the report points out how full or partial immigration bans on nationals from 39 countries, brought in by presidential proclamation, put international students and scholars in a “precarious” position.

And in India, the report highlights that Banaras Hindu University was one of a number of institutions to cancel a speaking engagement on account of external influence, axing a lecture by scholar Kedar Mishra “because the government opposed his participation.”

But public pressure also played a part in reducing academic liberty in 2025–26, the report says. Examples include the suspension or firing of several faculty members in the U.S. and Canada because of their public statements in the wake of the killing of political commentator Charlie Kirk last September.

And in January this year, the University of Arkansas announced that it had rescinded an offer to legal scholar Emily Suski to serve as the dean of its law school, stating that the decision was influenced by feedback from elected officials about Suski’s signing of an amicus brief filed with the U.S. Supreme Court, which supported transgender students’ right to play on sports teams aligned with their gender identity.

Nonetheless, the report also expresses “cautious optimism” about how new political administrations in Bangladesh and Hungary might reverse some of the more worrying developments for academic freedom.

Under Hungary’s new leader, Péter Magyar, who defeated far-right prime minister Viktor Orbán in April 2026, there is an opportunity to start “restoring university autonomy,” the report finds.

Under Orbán, public universities were put under political control by transferring their ownership to foundations headed by political appointees—in retaliation for which Hungary was suspended from the Erasmus student exchange program, as well as Horizon Europe. But “by the end of May, less than a month after Magyar took office, Hungary had indicated it would phase out the private foundation university model and rejoin the Erasmus student exchange programme,” the report notes.

Still, Robert Quinn, founding executive director of SAR, told Times Higher Education that the cases of freedom violations documented in the report were “just the tip of the iceberg.”

Speaking at the European Association for International Education conference in Glasgow last week, he said that efforts to defend academic freedom had never been stronger—but that the “bad news is that threats are growing faster than the efforts to protect.”

Quinn described ambitions to create a “global academic freedom agenda” to “change the tide” on intellectual and research liberty. The agenda must be “concrete and practical,” he said, and not simply “flowery language,” with an emphasis on creating clear parameters for how to protect and encourage academic freedom and intellectual debate.

He also said it was important in this regard to enlist the help of the general public by emphasizing the ways in which universities help them.

“The university that is in service to the public needs to [deliver a] message that it is in service to the public,” he said. “I think that’s the part we haven’t been doing. [Universities are] just not talking about it to the public in a way that the public understands.

“I believe if we spend the next 25 years really messaging that properly and absorbing those messages ourselves—that the public is our primary purpose—then the public will also be our primary defender.”

full_text:
Candidates contesting the Victorian state election for One Nation include a former Liberal who has won support from alleged underworld figures, a naturopath who has endorsed Donald Trump’s unfounded claim that paracetamol is linked to autism and a former shire councillor who lost his licence for drink-driving.

Pauline Hanson announced who would be her party’s upper house candidates and Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, at a press conference last month. Since then One Nation has used social media to unveil a steady stream of candidates, with 51 of the 88 lower house spots now filled.

Among them is Michael Piastrino, who launched his campaign on Sunday for the outer-suburban seat of Berwick, held by the Liberal Brad Battin on a 4.7% margin.

The launch was attended by Malaki Salesui, who was convicted in 2021 for his role in an organised car-theft ring.

Mick Mantzaris commented on photographs of the event on Instagram, writing: “great day great people” and “time for a change”. Mantzaris pleaded guilty in 2012 to possessing testosterone, disclosing restricted information and misleading the office of police integrity. The following year he was targeted in a drive-by shooting. Police described him at the time as “an associate of some outlaw motorcycle gang members”.

Anthony Younan, the nephew of the slain underworld figure Nabil Maghnie, also commented on Piastrino’s Instagram posts, saying he would vote for One Nation because of him: “I can’t believe I am going to vote for a red headed woman who hate Arabs. My mother is going to disown me Michael. But I am doing this for you bro!”

Piastrino, a hairdresser, ran for the Liberals at the 2022 election. He was forced to apologise during that campaign after declaring that Daniel Andrews would be “brought to justice for the murder of 800 people” under a Liberal government.

He told the Cranbourne Star News last month that he had met Mantzaris and Salesui through church. “I’m not here to judge people,” he said. “I’m here to help people.”

Sources have told Guardian Australia that One Nation has strengthened its candidate vetting process in the lead-up to the November election, with more stringent background checks and lengthy interviews.

In an interview in June, Kelvin Morton, One Nation’s general manager, said the party had also employed technology that did a “very comprehensive deep dive” into potential candidates’ social media accounts and provided a “thorough assessment” of their characters.

One Nation has also shown a willingness to accept candidates with controversial histories, including Pickering, who this month acknowledged past drug use and drink-driving.

Ben Lucas, the party’s candidate for the Liberal-held seat of Narracan, resigned from Baw Baw shire council in 2021 after being convicted of drink-driving and dangerous driving.

Court records seen by Guardian Australia show he was fined $2,000 and had his licence suspended for two years.

This month he pleaded guilty to operating a category-one aquatic facility without registering it with the council and was ordered to pay $3,000 in costs.

Lucas described the charges, which related to the operation of ice baths at his gym, on Facebook as a “storm in a teacup” that had been “blown out of proportion”. He said they arose from an “administrative oversight” involving the registration of his business after it moved.

“If I wasn’t involved with One Nation, would this have still been pursued in the same way?” he wrote.

Several One Nation candidates have deleted or scrubbed their social media accounts since announcing their candidacies, including Elita Dabrowski, who is contesting Sunbury, a seat Labor fears it could lose.

A deleted tweet, seen by Guardian Australia, shows Dabrowski backed Trump’s claim that paracetamol is linked to autism.

“This morning I watched Trump’s announcement on autism, vaccination schedules & paracetamol,” she wrote on 23 September 2025. “As a naturopath & functional health practitioner, I felt proud – it reflects what I see in clinic every day.”

Trump had said pregnant women should limit their use of the medication, claiming it heightens the risk of autism in children – an assertion disputed by scientists.

Meanwhile, Tammy Lindrum, One Nation’s candidate for the historically safe Labor seat of Albert Park, has left a trail of comments on Meta’s Threads about Muslim and First Nations people.

Under the handle “Lindrum Legends” and the username Tam Lindrum, she responded in April 2025 to a since-deleted post, saying there was “Black and Muslim supremacy in Australia” and that “the Whitman [sic] can’t say anything as they risk being accused of being racist”. Three months later, responding to another post, she wrote: “If you don’t like Bacon go back to a Muslim country.”

Responding to a post about plans to make the First Peoples’ Assembly of Victoria permanent, she wrote: “For a minority group I think we are going a little too far.

“We have paid their housing, welfare, education, health, for many years. When does that stop?”

Among candidates announced this week is Bruce Whalley, who blamed children for the climate crisis in tweet posted during the 2019 student strikes for climate action.

“Climate change is the fault of kids,” he wrote. “Stop asking for a car lift to school. WALK! RIDE a BIKE! or CATCH PUBLIC TRANSPORT. Gosh! Start to be a generation of doers Not talkers and complainers.”

title: Jantar Mantar protest fuelled interest but money, muscle persist in DU politics: students
summary: The elections are usually dominated by the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad and the National Students’ Union of India
full_text:
As students went to cast their votes on Friday, some said the large-scale protests at Jantar Mantar encouraged many to “raise their voices” and take an interest in student politics. However, pointing to thousands of pamphlets strewn on the roads and showing videos of male students harassing women, they said the DUSU elections remained largely a “money-muscle” game.

The elections are usually dominated by the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad and the National Students’ Union of India. This year, the Left joint panel of the All India Students’ Association and the Students’ Federation of India, along with the AAP’s Association of Students for Alternative Politics, hope to carry the Jantar Mantar momentum into the elections.

The Left has campaigned on the claim that “progressive forces” have been at the forefront of struggles such as those at Jantar Mantar and the Satya Niketan protests and therefore have a head start. Many university students attended the Jantar Mantar protest for educational reforms.

Issues and voting

While some students said they preferred to vote based on issues, many said they voted for friends or people they knew.

Sejal Kapoor, a first-year master’s student, said she had voted, but the “throwing of pamphlets, harassment of women students and whistling” made students less interested in politics. She said, “After Jantar Mantar, many students were inspired to take a stand.”

On the other hand, Muskan, who said she goes by her first name and is also a master’s student, said although she did not attend the Jantar Mantar protest, she identified with some of the issues raised there. “I am trying to appear for exams like Staff Selection Commission. When I reached 30 seconds late, I wasn’t allowed to enter. This is ironic because they themselves cancel papers and spoil the entire system,” she said.

The students, however, said such issues had barely featured in the election campaign. They also discussed which organisations had participated in the protests and which had not, but said this was unlikely to influence the outcome of the elections.

A cleaner DUSU

A group of students from the School of Open Learning and the Non-Collegiate Women’s Education Board (NCWEB) protested for a cleaner DUSU. Jyoti, an NCWEB student associated with the Krantikari Yuva Sangathan, said, “Just a few minutes ago, a male student made lewd gestures at us. They throw pamphlets around despite the guidelines and look for reasons to touch women students. This is how the money-muscle game works here.”

Himanshi, a first-year student at Hansraj College, did not vote. “There is no point voting because nobody really raises our issues. Hostels remain shut; we have gaushalas (cowsheds) in college instead of hostels, but nobody speaks about this,” she said.

title: The other side of China’s TNE story: China’s universities go overseas
summary:
What does the opening of a new Chinese university campus in Uzbekistan tell us about the changing TNE landscape in Central Asia and China’s own overseas ambitions? David Prentice explains.

The post The other side of China’s TNE story: China’s universities go overseas appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Much has been discussed recently about new transnational education (TNE) developments in China. Yet comparatively little attention has been paid to the delivery of China-led TNE programmes overseas, and the expansion of Chinese universities internationally.

However, the recent opening of a new branch campus in Uzbekistan illustrates how Chinese universities are starting to pay greater attention to establishing their own higher education provision outside China.

In August, Liaoning Normal University announced the opening of a new branch campus in Khiva, in the Khorezm region of Uzbekistan. The university has established the campus jointly with Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Innovation and Urgench State University.

The new campus has been designed to accommodate up to 2,000 students, with programs in tourism management, international business, artificial intelligence and Chinese language and culture. Uzbekistan’s government has allocated 140 billion Uzbek Soms (approximately USD$11.8 million) towards its construction.

TNE, and specifically the introduction of international branch campuses (IBCs), is increasingly being used across Central Asia to expand higher education capacity, strengthen quality, and develop skills for the region’s growing population.

In Uzbekistan, the number of international higher education institutions has increased rapidly, and the country now hosts the third largest concentration of IBCs globally after China and the UAE. The country’s 2026 higher education data currently record 35 foreign institutions in operation from countries like South Korea, India, Russia, and the UK.

The majority of these institutions are concentrated in Tashkent City and the Tashkent region, with only a small number located elsewhere in the country, including in Fergana, Andijan, and Samarkand. The new campus in Khiva is a significant addition as it’s not only as an expansion of Uzbekistan’s TNE provision, but also extends this model beyond the country’s main higher education centres while bringing a Chinese university into the landscape.

Kazakhstan has pursued a similar strategy in recent years, attracting international universities as part of its own efforts to expand and internationalise its higher education system. The country has welcomed providers including Cardiff University, which opened a branch campus in Astana in 2025, in addition to several other UK universities. Alongside this broader expansion of TNE, Kazakhstan has also developed deeper bilateral higher education ties with neighbouring China.

A number of joint institutions between Chinese universities and local universities have been established, including Beijing Language and Culture University‘s Astana campus, which opened in 2024 in partnership with Astana International University, and Northwestern Polytechnical University‘s Almaty branch campus, which opened in 2023 in partnership with Al-Farabi Kazakh National University. This growing institutional presence has been accompanied by increasing flows of international students into China, with around 20,000 Kazakhstani students studying in China as of 2025.

The new Khiva campus cannot be seen as an isolated development; it forms part of a small but growing presence of Chinese universities overseas

Within this context, the new Khiva campus cannot be seen as an isolated development; it forms part of a small but growing presence of Chinese universities overseas. Much of the recent discussion around Chinese TNE has focused on the other direction of travel, with foreign universities establishing programmes and campuses in China. This activity continues to expand, and in May 2026, China’s Ministry of Education approved 219 new Sino-foreign TNE partnerships – 133 joint programmes and 86 joint institutes. Less attention has been paid, however, to Chinese universities expanding their footprint overseas.

Current Chinese-led TNE takes several different forms. There are a small number of comprehensive branch campuses. Soochow University in Laos opened in the southeast Asian country in 2012. Xiamen University Malaysia also opened its doors in 2015 as the first overseas branch campus established by a Chinese university included in China’s Double First-Class Initiative.

However, the more common model for Chinese universities is embedded campuses within local institutions, as seen with Beijing Language and Culture University in Astana and Northwestern Polytechnical University in Almaty. This overseas presence is now growing as Chinese universities are increasingly encouraged to “go global”.

Chinese universities have historically operated within a highly centralised, state-directed system, with universities expected to align higher education to support the country’s development. However, changes in recent years have given universities greater autonomy in key areas, including in international collaboration. The result is a system that still involves strong government oversight, and where alignment with national development goals remains important, but gives universities more autonomy in how they pursue those goals, including through activities outside China.

Xi’an Shiyou University’s planned campus in Uzbekistan is a further example of how these broader strategic priorities are playing out in practice. The China-Uzbekistan Petroleum University as it will be known is being jointly developed in partnership with Samarkand State University and Uzbekistan Datang International Investment Co., the local subsidiary of the Chinese state-owned energy company China Datang Corporation. The campus will focus on energy-related education, while Datang’s first overseas renewable energy project in Uzbekistan also signals Central Asia’s growing importance to China’s energy security.

This is taking place alongside a rapid expansion of Chinese investment across Central Asia, particularly in energy and infrastructure, as the region has become an increasingly important part of the Belt and Road Initiative. In Uzbekistan’s Khorezm region, where the new Khiva campus is being established, Chinese investment is also growing. The province is currently home to 38 major projects backed by Chinese investors worth a combined $2.343 billion. These projects require skilled professionals with relevant technical skills and Chinese language ability, creating a clear role for institutions such as the new Khiva campus.

While TNE globally is already moving toward a model where it becomes much more closely linked to host nations’ economic and social development, the Chinese model offers an example of how this can be pursued. Chinese universities are increasingly becoming part of wider economic relationships, creating a model of TNE that is closely connected to countries where China has established commercial and strategic interests.

As this model develops, the growth of intra-Asian TNE will be an increasingly important part of the global TNE landscape.

title: Putting Pakistan on the TNE map: Beaconhouse International College and the future of global education
summary:
As the international education landscape shifts, TNE offers a way to provide high-quality options for families in their home country, write Safia Cassim and Ammaar Bin Saleem.

The post Putting Pakistan on the TNE map: Beaconhouse International College and the future of global education appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
For decades, international education has largely been associated with students crossing borders to access globally recognised universities. But that model is facing new pressures.

According to the UK Home Office’s latest immigration statistics, the number of Pakistani main applicants granted UK study visas fell by 47% year-on-year in the 12 months ending June 2026.

At the same time, the financial equation remains challenging: at an interbank exchange rate of approximately PKR 375 to £1 on 3 September 2026, an international tuition fee of £20,000 per year amounts to around PKR 7.5 million annually, or PKR 22.5 million over a typical three-year UK undergraduate degree, before accommodation and living expenses. For students and families in Pakistan, these realities are making alternative routes to a global education increasingly relevant.

TNE offers one answer, allowing students to access international qualifications while remaining in their home countries and, in some cases, reducing the tuition cost of an international degree by around 80% compared with studying overseas

Transnational education (TNE) offers one answer, allowing students to access international qualifications while remaining in their home countries and, in some cases, reducing the tuition cost of an international degree by around 80% compared with studying overseas. It also creates new opportunities for universities to engage with markets beyond their physical campuses.

Pakistan: A market that illustrates the shift

Pakistan has a long-standing relationship with the UK education system. The widespread recognition of O- and A-Level qualifications has created generations of students familiar with UK curricula and looking towards UK universities for higher education.

Beaconhouse has been part of this international outlook for decades. With a presence across eight countries and an education network serving more than 315,000 students, it has helped connect Pakistani learners with global education and opportunities.

Beaconhouse International College (BIC) represents the next stage of this journey: creating access to international higher education within Pakistan itself.

From international partnerships to TNE at scale

BIC has built its TNE model around three commitments: international academic access, industry readiness and entrepreneurship, underpinned by a strong focus on quality.

As Pakistan’s first and only ISO-certified TNE institute, BIC has established partnerships with the University of Essex, University of Kent, University of London, Liverpool John Moores University and Pearson, creating access to internationally recognised education within Pakistan.

But access is only the starting point. BIC connects classroom learning with the world of work through internships, its BIC Core Programme, which brings industry experts into the classroom, and programme clubs/student societies that give students practical professional exposure.

Students also participate in Collaborative Online International Learning (COIL) projects, developing experience of working and collaborating across borders. Alongside this, BIC Foundry provides a platform for students to develop and incubate their own ventures, taking ideas towards investment and the market.

Together, these dimensions position TNE as more than a route to an international qualification: it can connect global academic standards with quality, industry, international collaboration, employment and entrepreneurship.

From student mobility to global talent

The next opportunity for TNE in Pakistan is to move beyond access and towards impact. As Pakistan’s first and only ISO-certified TNE institute, BIC sees quality as the foundation for this ambition. Pakistan should not be viewed only as a market from which international students are recruited, but as a significant source of talent for the global workforce. For BIC, this means ensuring that our graduates are equipped to pursue opportunities both within Pakistan and beyond its borders.

We would like to see greater international career recruitment from Pakistan, with global organisations actively recognising and recruiting the talent being developed here. BIC is keen to partner with international employers and organisations to create these pathways, connecting our graduates with opportunities across markets and strengthening the relationship between international education and global employment.

In that sense, TNE is not replacing student mobility. It is expanding what international education can mean: giving students access to global education in Pakistan while enabling them to build careers in an increasingly borderless world.

About the authors:

Safia Cassim is country head of Beaconhouse International College. She is an experienced education professional with a career spanning several decades across the education sector. She currently serves as country head at Beaconhouse International College and has previously held senior leadership positions as regional director with leading education networks in Pakistan.

Ammaar Bin Saleem is head of marketing and communications at Beaconhouse International College. He has been serving the education sector for over a decade, with experience across education, marketing, communications and institutional branding. He currently leads marketing and communications at Beaconhouse International College, focusing on brand strategy, institutional communications and strengthening the organisation’s positioning in the international education space.

title: Why AI-Driven Modern Classrooms Require a Major Security Conversation
full_text:
The Modern Classroom Is Now the Cybersecurity Attack Surface

Identity gets baked right into the room too. I work with campuses where faculty tap their ID card to get into a building and then use that same card to log in to the AV system. A professor walks in, scans their college ID and their profile loads. Convenient? Sure. But the interactive panel is now part of the access control conversation. Who’s allowed to log in? What happens to their content afterward? How long does that credential stay live?

These concerns aren’t rhetorical or theoretical. Higher ed IT continues to see exploited vulnerabilities as the leading cause of ransomware attacks, at 35%, according to a Sophos survey. Unknown security gaps were the most commonly perceived organizational root cause, at 49%, for higher education institutions.

AI and Compliance Are Raising the Bar for Digital Safety

Artificial intelligence has made those questions more pressing. If a classful of students fires up AI tools on their laptops or smartphones all at once, the network must be able to handle that traffic. And whatever those tools are doing with student data needs to be safe and compliant. Which devices are on which networks? What kind of bandwidth and latency can we guarantee? How are we protecting student data under the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act and other compliance mandates?

DISCOVER: Artificial intelligence has made identity security more important than ever.

Those are network engineering questions as much security questions, and they are showing up in general-purpose classrooms now, not just in labs.

Research and lab spaces illustrate these security considerations in concrete ways. I’ve worked on projects where grant language dictates the types of cameras we can use, down to the refresh rates, the latency, video storage and what kind of physical access control is on the lab door. If the grant lasts eight years, we must think about the technology of 2034 when we’re buying it in 2026. That includes the security posture of every device we hang on a wall or put in a rack.

So, yes, on paper I’m in the classroom modernization business. But when I’m looking at a room layout now, including where the displays go, what kind of audio we use, which boards and cameras we specify, I’m also looking at a security diagram: Who taps in where, what’s talking to what, and how will this space behave when something goes wrong, not just when everything goes right.

Every Campus Has a Tie-Breaker When It Comes to Digital Safety

Higher ed institutions fall into a few categories when it comes to these questions:

Identity-driven schools have established what they want to be known for. For a journalism powerhouse such as the University of Missouri, or a broadcast school such as Syracuse University or Northwestern University, the studios, lecture halls and production classrooms that support it are part of its public face. If the cameras, control rooms and capture spaces in those buildings aren’t secure and reliable, the university isn’t just risking a bad Tuesday class, it’s risking the school’s reputation and brand.

LEARN MORE: AV-over-IP technology makes classrooms easier to manage.

Research and public-private campuses — including Ivy League schools, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the Research Triangle schools in North Carolina — are downstream of National Science Foundation and National Institutes of Health funding and hospital partnerships. These are nonnegotiable as they are written into the funding.

Comprehensive campuses have the hardest job, I think. For a campus that has 8,000 students and 40 majors that all matter equally, their decision-making can be further complicated without having a marquee program to default to. So, what breaks the tie when everything is competing for the same modernization budget?

Increasingly, it’s security, and the institutions doing this well are turning it into an advantage instead of a constraint.

What Bowie State Got Right With Cloud-Based Surveillance

Bowie State University had a fragmented infrastructure with cameras that didn’t talk to one another. Instead of asking for a tech refresh or expensive camera equipment, the IT team partnered with the university’s Department of Public Safety and pitched a unified, campuswide physical security strategy to build a modern, command-center environment: a cloud-managed platform with a single-pane-of-glass dashboard that both IT and security can access.

WATCH: Bowie State University’s physical security strategy streamlines operations.

It cut the maintenance burden, too, as it freed the team from having to do manual software upgrades, server patches and physical troubleshooting.

When deciding what to fund in 2026, safety and security increasingly are becoming prioritized considerations. There is always a compliance piece, and that has intensified post-pandemic. Whether they are working on a large networking project or a single classroom upgrade, IT directors are prioritizing campus safety when deciding what aspects of the internal infrastructure will get upgraded for compliance and security — and rightfully so.
